question: What are Spring bean scopes?
title: Spring Bean Scopes Overview
direct_answer: **Bean scope** defines how many instances of a bean Spring creates and how long they live. The five scopes are: **singleton** (default — one per context), **prototype** (new per injection), **request** (one per HTTP request), **session** (one per HTTP session), **application** (one per ServletContext).

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of all bean scopes and their use cases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing singleton and prototype, not the web scopes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the N+1 scope problem: injecting a prototype into a singleton

sections.title: Scope Annotation
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Spring has five bean scopes. Singleton is the default — one shared instance per application context. This works perfectly for stateless services like `UserService` or `ProductRepository`. Prototype creates a new instance every time the bean is requested — useful for stateful beans or when you need a fresh object per operation. Then there are three web scopes: request creates one instance per HTTP request, session creates one per user session — useful for things like a shopping cart, and application creates one per the servlet context. For most Spring Boot backends, you'll use singleton for services and occasionally prototype. The web scopes are more relevant for traditional Spring MVC with sessions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Scope answers one question: how many copies of this bean should exist, and for how long?

beats.text: Bean scope controls how many instances Spring creates for a given bean definition and how long those instances live. It's declared with @Scope on the class or @Bean method. Spring picks the right scope automatically for singleton — it's the default — and you opt into other scopes explicitly.

Different beans have different lifetimes. A stateless UserService can safely be shared across every request — one instance is enough. A stateful ReportBuilder that accumulates data during processing needs a fresh instance per use. Web apps need beans tied to HTTP request or session boundaries. Scope is how you express these different requirements.

items: singleton (default): one instance per ApplicationContext, shared everywhere. Works for stateless beans.
prototype: new instance every time the bean is injected or requested. Use for stateful beans.
request: one instance per HTTP request. Destroyed when the request ends.
session: one instance per user HTTP session. Lives until the session expires.
application: one instance per ServletContext — similar to singleton but scoped to the web app.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, OrderService is singleton by default — Spring creates it once and injects the same instance into every controller and service that needs it. If we add a ReportBuilder that collects line items during a build operation, we annotate it @Scope("prototype") so each call to generate a report gets a fresh, empty builder. sharp edge: injecting a prototype into a singleton breaks prototype semantics — the singleton only gets one prototype instance at startup. Use ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> to get a fresh instance each time.

items: Don't store per-request or per-user data in a singleton field — concurrent requests will overwrite each other's data.
Web scopes (request, session) require proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS when injected into singletons, otherwise the singleton gets the wrong instance.

speakable_v2.cap: Singleton for stateless beans, prototype for stateful ones, web scopes for HTTP-lifecycle data — get the scope right and thread safety takes care of itself.

question: What is the singleton bean scope in Spring?
title: Spring Singleton Bean Scope
direct_answer: **Singleton** is the default scope — Spring creates exactly one instance per `ApplicationContext` and shares it wherever the bean is injected. It's ideal for stateless service classes (`@Service`, `@Repository`). Note: singleton scope is per context, not per JVM.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the most common bean scope
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying singleton means one per JVM — it's one per ApplicationContext
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why singleton beans must be stateless (thread safety)

sections.title: Singleton Scope Details
sections.content:
In Spring's singleton scope, one bean instance is created and **shared across all injection points**. When 10 different classes `@Autowire` a `UserService`, they all get the same `UserService` instance. This is different from the GoF Singleton pattern — Spring singletons are per `ApplicationContext`, not per JVM. Two application contexts in the same JVM would have two `UserService` instances.

**Thread safety requirement**: since one instance serves all requests simultaneously, singleton beans must be stateless — no instance variables that change per request.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Default scope for all Spring beans
- One instance **per ApplicationContext** (not per JVM)
- All injections get the same instance
- **Must be stateless** — no mutable instance fields (thread safety!)
- Storing request data in singleton fields = bug under concurrent requests
- Created at startup (eager by default)
- `@Scope("singleton")` or `@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_SINGLETON)`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Singleton scope means Spring creates one instance and shares it everywhere the bean is needed. It's the default, so your `@Service` and `@Repository` classes are all singletons. The important point about singleton beans is that they must be stateless. Since the same instance handles all requests concurrently, if you stored any request-specific data in an instance field, you'd have a race condition. Keep your services stateless — pass data through method parameters, don't store it as fields. One thing interviewers sometimes trip people up on: Spring singleton is per ApplicationContext, not per JVM — a distinction from the classic Singleton design pattern.

speakable_v2.hook: One instance, shared by everyone — singleton is the default for a reason, but it only works if your bean doesn't hold state.

beats.text: Singleton scope means Spring creates exactly one instance of the bean per ApplicationContext and reuses it for every injection. All @Autowired references to that type point to the same object. It's the default scope — you don't need @Scope("singleton") unless you're being explicit.

Stateless service beans have no per-request data to protect. Creating a new UserService for every HTTP request would waste memory and time. One shared instance is just as correct and far more efficient — singleton is the natural scope for stateless objects.

items: One instance per ApplicationContext — not per JVM. Two contexts in the same JVM each have their own singleton instance.
Created eagerly at startup by default — all configuration errors surface immediately.
Shared concurrently — all threads access the same object, so it must be stateless.
Distinct from the GoF Singleton design pattern — Spring singleton is container-managed, not enforced at the class level.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, OrderService is a singleton. Every controller that injects it gets the same instance. The service's methods take an Order parameter, process it, delegate to a repository, and return a result — no state stored in fields. candidates miss: the moment you add a private field like private User currentUser to store request-specific data, you've created a concurrency bug. Two requests running simultaneously will overwrite each other's currentUser.

items: Storing mutable state in a singleton field is a classic concurrency bug — use method parameters or ThreadLocal, never instance fields for request data.
Spring singleton is not the GoF Singleton — don't add a private constructor or a getInstance() method to your Spring beans.

speakable_v2.cap: Singleton is right for any bean whose methods are pure functions of their inputs — no stored state means no shared-state bugs.

question: What is the prototype bean scope and when do you use it?
title: Spring Prototype Bean Scope
direct_answer: **Prototype** scope creates a **new bean instance every time** it's injected or requested via `getBean()`. Use it for stateful beans, command objects, or any bean where sharing an instance would cause correctness issues. Spring does NOT call `@PreDestroy` on prototype beans.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding when shared singleton state causes problems
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Spring doesn't manage @PreDestroy for prototype beans
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton problem and how to solve it with ObjectProvider or @Lookup

sections.title: When to Use Prototype
sections.content:
Use prototype scope when:
1. **Stateful beans**: a bean that accumulates state per use (e.g., a `ReportBuilder` that collects data and generates a report — you need a fresh one per report)
2. **Non-thread-safe beans**: beans that use non-thread-safe collaborators
3. **Command/Strategy objects**: different configurations per call

**Warning — Prototype in Singleton problem**: if you `@Autowire` a prototype bean into a singleton, you only get ONE prototype instance because the singleton is injected once at startup.

sections.title: Correct Prototype Usage with ObjectProvider
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Prototype scope gives you a new instance every time the bean is injected or requested. It's useful for stateful beans where sharing an instance would cause bugs — like a report builder that accumulates state during its work. The gotcha is what I call the prototype-in-singleton problem: if you `@Autowire` a prototype bean directly into a singleton, you only get one prototype instance because the singleton is only injected once at startup. To get a fresh prototype each time, you use `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` and call `getObject()` whenever you need a fresh instance. Also worth knowing: Spring doesn't call `@PreDestroy` on prototype beans, so you're responsible for cleanup.

followup_questions: Does Spring call @PreDestroy on prototype beans?

seo.metaTitle: Spring Prototype Bean Scope | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn Spring prototype bean scope, when to use it for stateful beans, the prototype-in-singleton problem, and how to use ObjectProvider for fresh instances.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Prototype gives you a fresh bean every single time — but injecting it into a singleton silently hands you the same old instance.

beats.text: Prototype scope means Spring creates a new bean instance every time the bean is injected or fetched via getBean(). There's no shared instance. Spring creates the bean, injects its dependencies, and then hands it to you — after that, you're responsible for it. Spring doesn't track it further and won't call @PreDestroy when you're done.

Some beans accumulate state during their operation. A ReportBuilder that collects line items while building a report can't be shared — each report needs its own clean builder. Prototype scope solves this by making every injection a fresh start.

items: New instance per injection: every @Autowired point that declares a prototype bean gets its own copy.
New instance per getBean(): calling applicationContext.getBean(Type.class) on a prototype also creates a fresh instance.
No @PreDestroy: Spring doesn't manage prototype bean destruction — release resources manually if needed.
ObjectProvider<T> as a factory: injecting ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> lets a singleton get a new prototype on every getObject() call.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, ReportBuilder is @Scope("prototype"). ReportService injects ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> via constructor. Each call to generateReport() calls builderProvider.getObject() to get a fresh, empty builder, builds the report, and discards the builder. production trap: if ReportService had @Autowired ReportBuilder directly, Spring would inject one prototype at startup and ReportService would reuse that same builder for every report — corrupting results for concurrent requests.

items: Don't @Autowired a prototype directly into a singleton — it defeats the purpose. Use ObjectProvider or @Lookup method injection.
You're responsible for cleanup of prototype beans — if they hold resources like file handles, close them explicitly.

speakable_v2.cap: Prototype gives you a truly fresh bean, but only if you fetch it through ObjectProvider — direct @Autowired in a singleton is a trap.

question: What are request and session scopes in Spring?
title: Request and Session Scopes in Spring
direct_answer: **Request scope**: one bean instance per HTTP request — bean is created when request starts and destroyed when it ends. **Session scope**: one bean instance per HTTP session — lives for the user's session lifetime. Both require `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS` when injected into singletons.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing proxyMode is required when injecting web-scoped beans into singletons
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a realistic session scope example: shopping cart, user preferences

sections.title: Request and Session Scope Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Request**: one instance per HTTP request, thread-safe (each request has own instance)
- **Session**: one instance per user session (HttpSession)
- **proxyMode**: required when injecting into a singleton — Spring injects a proxy that delegates to the right scope
- Without proxy: singleton gets one instance at startup, not per-request/session
- REST APIs with JWT (stateless): typically don't use session scope
- Session scope needs session support configured (Spring Session or container sessions)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request — perfect for storing request-specific context that you want available throughout the request pipeline without passing it everywhere. Session scope is one instance per user's HTTP session — the classic use case is a shopping cart that persists across multiple requests from the same user. The key thing when using these scopes is `proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS`. Because singleton beans are created once at startup, injecting a request-scoped bean directly into a singleton won't work — the singleton only gets one instance. The proxy mode tells Spring to inject a proxy that transparently delegates to the correct request or session instance at runtime.

followup_questions: Why is proxyMode required for web-scoped beans in singletons?
Why wouldn't you use session scope in a stateless REST API?

seo.metaTitle: Spring Request Session Bean Scopes | Java Interview Questions for Freshers

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Request and session scopes tie a bean's lifetime to the HTTP lifecycle — one for a single request, one for the whole user session.

groups.heading: Request scope
groups.text: One bean instance per HTTP request. It's created when the request arrives and destroyed when the response is sent. Each request gets its own instance, so storing per-request data is completely thread-safe. Useful for request context objects you want available throughout the filter-controller-service chain.

groups.heading: Session scope
groups.text: One bean instance per user HTTP session. It survives across multiple requests from the same user and lives until the session expires. The classic use case is a shopping cart — items added across several page visits persist in the same bean instance.

items: Use request scope when you need per-request data flowing through multiple layers without passing it as method parameters.
Use session scope for user-specific stateful data that must survive across multiple requests — like a multi-step checkout.
Don't use session scope in stateless REST APIs with JWT — there's no server-side session to bind to.

beats.text: gotcha: both scopes need proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS when injected into a singleton. Without it, the singleton grabs one instance at startup — always the wrong request's or session's data. The proxy tells Spring to look up the real scoped bean per-request or per-session each time a method is called on it.

speakable_v2.cap: Request scope for per-call data, session scope for per-user state — and always add proxyMode when injecting either into a singleton.

question: What is the problem with injecting a prototype bean into a singleton in Spring?
title: Prototype Bean in Singleton Problem
direct_answer: When a prototype bean is injected into a singleton via `@Autowired`, the prototype is only created once (when the singleton is created). The singleton holds a reference to this single prototype instance forever, effectively making it behave like a singleton. This defeats the purpose of prototype scope.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing this is a problem and assuming prototype beans always get fresh instances
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all three solutions: ObjectProvider, @Lookup, ApplicationContext.getBean()

sections.title: The Problem and Solutions
ObjectProvider Solution (Recommended)
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: This is a classic Spring gotcha. When you `@Autowire` a prototype bean into a singleton, Spring creates the prototype bean ONCE when the singleton is created, and that's the only instance the singleton ever gets. So the prototype effectively becomes a singleton within that class. The right fix is to inject `ObjectProvider<MyPrototype>` instead — then every time you call `provider.getObject()`, you get a truly fresh instance. Another option is the `@Lookup` method annotation where Spring overrides a method in the singleton to always return a new prototype instance, but `ObjectProvider` is simpler and more common in modern Spring code.

followup_questions: Is it ever correct to directly @Autowire a prototype into a singleton?

seo.metaTitle: Prototype Bean in Singleton Problem | Java Spring Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn the prototype-in-singleton problem in Spring where a prototype injected into a singleton only creates one instance, and how to fix it with ObjectProvider.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: You marked it prototype, but the singleton only asked for it once — now everyone's sharing the 'fresh' instance you thought you'd get.

beats.text: The prototype-in-singleton problem is when a prototype-scoped bean is @Autowired directly into a singleton. Spring injects the prototype once — when it creates the singleton — and the singleton holds that same instance for its entire lifetime. Prototype semantics are completely lost. It behaves as if the bean were singleton.

Spring's injection wiring runs once at startup. The singleton asks for a TaskProcessor, Spring creates one prototype instance, injects it, and that's the end of injection for that field. There's no mechanism to re-inject the field on every method call — unless you explicitly design for it.

items: Wrong pattern: @Autowired TaskProcessor processor in a singleton — one prototype instance for the singleton's lifetime.
ObjectProvider fix (recommended): inject ObjectProvider<TaskProcessor> and call getObject() each time you need a fresh one.
@Lookup fix: annotate a protected abstract method — Spring overrides it to return a new prototype on every call.
ApplicationContext.getBean() fix: works but it's the Service Locator anti-pattern — avoid in production code.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, TaskService is singleton. TaskProcessor is @Scope("prototype") because it holds per-task mutable state. If TaskService @Autowires TaskProcessor directly, every task shares the same processor — state from task A bleeds into task B. The fix: inject ObjectProvider<TaskProcessor>. Each call to processorProvider.getObject() creates a brand new TaskProcessor. candidates miss: @Lookup also works — you declare protected abstract TaskProcessor createProcessor(); and Spring generates an implementation that creates a fresh prototype each time.

items: The bug is silent — Spring doesn't warn you that the prototype is being degraded to singleton behavior.
Don't use ApplicationContext.getBean() as the fix in your service layer — it's the Service Locator anti-pattern and makes testing harder.

speakable_v2.cap: Direct @Autowired of a prototype into a singleton silently breaks prototype semantics — always use ObjectProvider or @Lookup to get a fresh instance.

question: What is the default scope for Spring beans and why?
title: Why Singleton Is the Default Spring Bean Scope
direct_answer: **Singleton is the default** because most Spring beans are stateless services where sharing an instance is safe and efficient. Creating a new service instance per injection would waste memory and initialization time. Singleton is the correct choice for any stateless bean.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of why singleton was chosen as default
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not being able to explain the reasoning behind singleton as default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to thread safety in a multi-threaded web server environment

sections.title: Why Singleton Makes Sense as Default
sections.content: Web applications handle many concurrent requests. Service classes like `UserService`, `OrderService`, `ProductRepository` are **stateless** — they don't store any per-request data in their fields, they just process inputs and return outputs. For stateless objects, there's no reason to create multiple instances. One instance can safely serve all requests concurrently. Creating a new `UserService` per request would be wasteful — it would need to be instantiated, have its dependencies injected, and then be garbage collected, for every single request.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Stateless beans = no mutable state = safe to share = singleton is perfect
- Memory efficiency: one instance vs thousands per hour
- Startup speed: initialized once vs per-request
- `@Repository` beans are stateless: just delegate to Hibernate/JDBC
- `@Service` beans are stateless: process input, call repository, return result
- Violation: storing user data in a service field → concurrency bug

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Singleton is the default because the vast majority of Spring beans are stateless. A `UserService` just has methods that take parameters, call the repository, and return results. There's no per-request state stored in the object itself. For stateless objects, one shared instance is just as correct as multiple instances, and it's far more efficient. Creating a new service bean per request would cause unnecessary object creation and garbage collection overhead. The rule of thumb is: if your bean has no mutable instance fields (or only final fields that are set once at construction), it's stateless and singleton is the right scope.

seo.metaDescription: Understand why singleton is the default Spring bean scope, how stateless services benefit from sharing one instance, and the efficiency rationale.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Singleton is the default because the right answer for stateless code is always 'share it — there's nothing to protect.'

beats.text: Singleton is the default Spring bean scope because the vast majority of Spring beans are stateless service objects. A stateless bean has no mutable instance fields — it receives inputs through method parameters and returns outputs without storing anything. For stateless objects, sharing one instance across all callers is completely safe and dramatically more efficient than creating a new instance for every injection or request.

Web servers handle hundreds or thousands of requests per second. If every request created a new UserService, that's thousands of object allocations per second, each with dependency injection, followed by garbage collection. Singleton eliminates all that overhead for beans where sharing is safe.

items: Stateless bean: no mutable instance fields — only final dependencies set in the constructor. Safe as singleton.
Memory efficiency: one instance shared by all callers vs one instance per caller per request.
Initialization cost: constructor and @PostConstruct run once at startup, not once per request.
Stateful bean: has mutable instance fields that differ per use — needs prototype scope.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, OrderService has two final fields: UserRepository and EmailService, both set in the constructor. The service methods take an Order parameter and return an OrderResult. There's zero per-request state stored in the object. Sharing one OrderService instance across all requests is perfectly safe — and it means Spring creates it once at startup instead of once per request. sharp edge: the moment you add a non-final mutable field to a singleton — say private List<Event> pendingEvents — you've created a concurrency bug. Two threads adding to the same list will corrupt each other's data.

items: Don't store mutable per-request data in singleton fields — it's a concurrency bug waiting to happen under load.
Don't assume all beans should be singleton — stateful objects like command builders or accumulators genuinely need prototype scope.

speakable_v2.cap: The rule is simple: no mutable instance state means singleton is safe and efficient — any mutable state signals you need a narrower scope.
